newsitem.title: USA: Dollar rises with stocks, bonds in election day rally.
newsitem.headline: Dollar rises with stocks, bonds in election day rally.

text.p: The dollar climbed against major currencies Tuesday along with stock and bond prices as currency traders bet Republicans would retain control of Congress even if President Clinton wins re-election.

Financial markets cheered the prospect of a Republican-led Congress that would keep pressure on the White House to balance the budget and block a second Clinton administration from sharply boosting government spending.

"I think people truly believe that the Democrats will not take over Congress, and at the very worst, it'll be a split, and at the very best, the Republicans will maintain control of both houses," said Ben Strauss, an assistant vice president of foreign exchange at Bank Julius Baer and Co.

The dollar surged to 114.30 Japanese yen and 1.2810 Swiss francs, a new 20-month high. It settled at 114.25 yen and 1.2765 francs late in New York, up from 113.80 yen and 1.2662 francs late on Monday.
The dollar climbed to 1.5200 German marks from 1.5105 marks.
Early election results were expected after polls closed at 6 p.m. EST (2300 GMT) in Kentucky and Indiana, with the polls in seven more states to close at 7 p.m. EST (midnight GMT).
Results of which party won majorities in the House and Senate could take longer because of time differences in the West, where there are many critical races.

The dollar's strong performance, especially against the Swiss franc, also partly reflected traders relief that Russian President Boris Yeltsin appeared to come through heart surgery successfully. Russian cardiologist Renat Akchurin, who led the surgical team, said Yeltsin should be fit enough in a few days to take back power from Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
The Swiss franc, often sought as a haven during political uncertainty, fell after the news about Yeltsin.
"As more and more of its safe haven role starts to diminish, then the question is why do you want to hold Swiss francs," said Diego Giurleo, vice president of Treasury at the Royal Bank of Canada.
Giurleo noted low Swiss interest rates also made the currency less attractive. Low rates can pressure a currency by making deposits denominated in that currency less desirable to foreign investors.
Speculation that official German interest rates will remain low weighed on the mark after the Economic Ministry said West German industrial orders tumbled in September from the previous month.

The German central bank has kept rates low to boost Germany's economy. Some central bank officials recently made remarks that left some currency traders thinking rates might rise in the not too distant future.
But the weak industrial orders report along with a decline in industrial output reported on Monday put to rest the notion of a rate increase.
"As a minimum, anybody looking for a rate hike in Germany, that concern has to be pushed off further in the future," said Ron Leven, currency strategist at J.P. Morgan.
The dollar lost ground to the Canadian dollar, which rose to its highest level in 13 months against its American counterpart.
The Canadian currency gained partly as the Canadian bond maket outperformed U.S. bonds, according to Anne Pankowski, a director of foreign exchange at Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce.
The dollar fell to Canadian $1.3305 from C$1.3361 on Monday. The British pound edged up to $1.6470 from $1.6453.
